title: Pluggable limiter algorithms
idea: An extensible rate limiter builds limiters from configuration through a registry of factories, and adds behavior by wrapping limiters in decorators instead of editing them.
points: A factory maps an algorithm name to a constructor; new names register at startup.
Config text such as a route's rule picks the algorithm without code changes.
A composite limiter allows a call only when every inner limiter allows it.
Decorators add metrics or an allow-list while the inner algorithm stays untouched.

hero.title: From config text to a wrapped limiter

edges.label: parsed by
edges.caption: The factory splits a route's rule text on plus signs and reads each algorithm name.

edges.label: builds
edges.caption: Each name looks up its registered maker, which builds one limiter from a rule and a clock.

edges.label: joined into
edges.caption: Two or more parts become a composite. A call passes only if every part allows it.

edges.label: wrapped by
edges.caption: A counting decorator records each answer. Decorators.java wraps a stand-in limiter; a composite wraps the same way.

edges.label: wrapped by
edges.caption: An outer allow-list returns early for exempt keys, so inner layers never see them.

code.title: Factory, config, composite
code.caption: Routes read their limiter from config text. A second algorithm is registered without touching the factory. `tryAcquire` returns a boolean here to keep the wiring short.

walk.text: Register algorithms by name. Sliding log arrives later with one line.
Config per route; upload combines a per-second and a per-minute rule.
Six calls per route: four at 0 ms, two at 1000 ms. Y means allowed.
An unknown algorithm fails at startup, not on the first request.
The registry maps names to constructors that take a rule and a clock.
Parse each part, look up its maker, and build one limiter per part.
Several parts become a composite: every part must allow the call.

code.title: Stacking decorators
code.caption: Metrics and an allow-list wrap any limiter. The order of wrapping decides what gets counted.

walk.text: Wrap the core in a counter, then wrap that in an allow-list.
Three calls from u1, three from ops, then print the counter.
The counter forwards every call and records the answer.
Exempt keys return early, so the inner limiter never sees them.

pitfalls: In a composite, earlier parts spend budget even when a later part rejects.
Validate the whole config at startup; a typo should stop the deploy.
Wrapping order matters: an outer allow-list hides exempt calls from inner metrics.

quiz.q: What is the last line Decorators prints?
quiz.why: The allow-list sits outside the counter. The three ops calls return early and are never counted; u1 gets two allows and one reject.

takeaway: Register new algorithms and wrap new behavior; never edit working limiters.

starters: How would I reload limiter config without restarting?
